blind_spots: Almost all evidence reflects artists/writers/designers hostile or skeptical toward AI; no voices from creators who successfully built repeatable systems and are satisfied, so the 'stopped chasing prompts in favor of building systems they can trust' behavior is asserted as a need but not documented in practice.
No quantitative data on how widespread the slot-machine frustration is — claims rely on 'a growing number' / 'many' without measured prevalence.
Much of the on-topic detail comes from a single synthesizer (Perplexity Sonar) paraphrasing or quoting sources; primary verbatim user complaints from named professionals are thin.
No evidence on specific tools, model versions, or whether features like fixed seeds already partially solve the problem — the pain is described generically.
Rights/licensing concerns ('rights-respecting') surface in the evidence but are entangled with the reproducibility pain and not separately explored as a workflow blocker.
Little on the 'win over AI' / overcoming the problem angle (the r/graphic_design row is a bare headline with no detail), leaving solution-side validation unsupported.
contradictions: The slot-machine randomness is framed as a pain/loss of craft by most sources, yet some community voices frame the same unpredictability as a thrill/'BIG HIT' and an addictive draw — pain for professionals but reward for casual users.
Creative Bloq argues the generic, prompt-limited nature of AI works in artists' favour (a positive), contradicting the dominant view that opacity and genericness are unmet needs/pains.

Ruben Hassid's framing leans into 'overload & addiction' and evolutionary variation ('thousands of variations — most fail, few survive') as a workflow he engages with, somewhat at odds with peers who reject prompt-chasing entirely in favor of deterministic systems.
